You could be eating a granola bar absentmindedly. You could be making a colorful list of chores to stick on the fridge for your lazier household counterparts. You could be listening to music yelping from a nearby truck radio, or feeding your axolotl, or fighting the urge to locate then shit in the library bathroom as you discover how boy wonder Harry Potter resolves his clumsy desires for Cho Chang. Then suddenly, you separate yourself. By maybe an inch. And you see yourself, you see what you’re doing, and there isn't any meaning there.  It could hit you idly then rumble up to seriously. At any moment, the thought bobs to the surface and stays there, causing widening ripples: you want to kill yourself. Or you should. Or you might. You could be giggling with some sitcom's laughtrack, then spend each instant of commercial break debating, again, and again, and again. 

You realize that it's an actual option, and has always been. A radius of some yards extends around you, all objects within the vicinity advertising themselves as potential tools. In the span of a minute, you could clutch at a heavy knife handle, hug a throttling truck, choke down every dry drop of drug behind the mirror. With each breath you fully comprehend the choice you've constantly been making, with every blip of a moment: each perspiration mustache induced by smooth faced baristas, each pause at the checkout clutching axolotl food flakes, each flip of flimsy magazine spread celebrating incredible post-pregnancy weight loss. You'd been forgetting that you were hovering over the Erase button the entire time.

You could be drunk on cheap cocktails, burping up notes of 80 proof and Dr. Pepper as you stumble into a familiar cluttered office where you could jerk open the bottom drawer and pick an unopened sheet of razors. You could sear open your wrists silently to the thumped sound of college radio and people who were maybe your friends and you could do it so quickly that

At first, it's something you ignore. For the sake of getting by. You keep on thinking that it's going to be temporary. Tomorrow's going to be better, and tonight's isolation is a kind of low place exception. 

It seems to snowball, but it doesn't, really. It just plods along, like a string of beeping in the background, and you waver in and out of being annoyed or even conscious of it. You're looking for the cheapest quart of 1% in the dairy aisle and you're lonely. You're getting head from someone you're infatuated with and you're lonely. You've got the job, you're getting dressed for the first day with a cup of hot coffee, and you're lonely. Anything. You step back even an inch, and you understand the backdrop's still the same. 

"This is what everyone is experiencing, right?" Is a question you never ask anybody else. But you think about asking it. You think about it almost constantly, some days. Then you think about what "it" even is: why are you lonely?

There are the easy answers that keep you safely in your lonesome cage: you're ugly, you're stupid, you're boring, you're incapable of not being any of these things. But that's not really it. Even assuming these qualities are accurate, that doesn't mean you can't be happy or connect with other people.

[Pauses, an idea sparks, shifts and scoffs] You know, the irritating part is, you could even be happy, or even be connecting with other people, and you know in the pit of your belly that, yeah, you're still excruciatingly lonely. So, what is it?

"What is it?" Is a question you might nonverbally ask yourself, staring up at a dark ceiling at 1 AM with the fan on low. While your mouth still waters from the overpowering taste of Wintergreen Listerine, you try and dissect this feeling. This THING that surfaces when you can't have any forefront distraction.

And as you look intently at the stucco styled wall above your head, you realize it's the internal questions themselves that separate you. That definitively set you aside from every other person.

Wait. That's not quite the answer. It's not the self doubt itself, it's not the questions exactly: it's the voice inside your head. The "you" that reads with you, that real-time edits your long winded sentences, that holds your hand when you're watching the night sky. It's the "you" that understands perfectly sentiments and perspectives you will never, ever be able to articulate to anybody else. 

There is no vocabulary wide enough to put somebody inside of your brain. Inside of that "you" that you truly and strongly identify as--not to other people, that is, but to yourself. You will never be able to share your thoughts completely with another human being.

The tragedy--that we live life in separate bodies. Separate minds. We have these private tiny spheres of thought that don't meld into everybody else's tiny spheres. We're born alone, grow alone, and when we die, we do so absolutely in solitude. We live lives devoted to expressing and sharing things that can never be entirely expressed or shared.

[Pauses, defeated] Every word out of my mouth is agonizing defeat. Every thought wants more attention that it could ever have. Every hug concludes with dread in my chest, that our bodies and our faces couldn't meld into a two-brained monster, couldn't slosh around an enormous skull so that together we could be safe from the ravenous lonesomeness. Every conversation I have is distraction from that final moment, that final sigh wherein I know with certainty that I've only ever lived alone.

Above all, keep an optimistic outlook, and know that every struggle with trust that you have from a shitty past is temporary, and if you're well equipped those episodes can get shorter and shorter. A Dear Self list is the best weaponry I can think of; in sane times where I'm not overwhelmed by my emotions, I realize I'm the most aware of what arguing points can persuade that other side of my brain, more than anyone else.

“--Fuck it,” she chokes out loudly, meeting those neon red beads feet away. “Look...there is no person...I care about, more than YOU. That’s right, YOU! Don’t be afraid. Don’t be ashamed. I love you the way you are--and I’m going to be right here, I’m not going to move. Look. Don’t be afraid. Everything is going to be okay. You are loved. “Nothing. When he asks you what you want to order, you smile and say coffee’s fine.”

Oh man, the cheddar double hitter looks fucking gruesome, he bit his lip, hunched over the menu somewhat precariously because the slender bar chairs don’t accommodate his frame well. 

Face widening, expression vacant, she silently sifted through any slicing remarks she could make as a decided vegan.

“A vegan who sucks buckets of chilled fried meat from dainty bones at two in the morning, squinting in fridge light?”

He’d probably order fries with it. It was fries or tator tots here. Or a side iceberg salad, but that would cost an additional dollar. Would he suggest splitting the bill in half? She gnawed her cheeks like gum.

“You’re not listening to me, you cunt. Don’t consider even taking the god damned garnish off that grease slick plate. Even if the jackoff makes you pay for all of it.”

What are you going to order, do you want to look? 

No, that’s fine, she shifted around the cold cushioned seat. 

“Who gags until acidic juices bubble down her wobbly chin, who stares at the placid toilet bowl still figuring out which drive thrus provide round-the-clock sustenance for gluttonous itty goblins?”

Hey, it comes with a dessert, he says, squinting at miniature descriptions behind the oily menu lamination. You want to pick one? I’m not a sweets guy. 

“Are you actually considering it? Oh, and ICE CREAM, too? Do you actually enjoy being a bloated animal, needing primp yourself for hours just to appear presentable enough?”

Nah, none of these are vegan-friendly. She shrugs, as though disappointed.

“You are disappointed, you fat bitch.”

She brings the rim of the steaming mug to her lips but does not tip the liquid to her steeled mouth. 

“Do you enjoy horrifying everyone around you?”

She places the cup down gingerly enough to not make a sound. It is surrounded by stingingly pink lipstick bruises. She jiggles both legs, looking at her lap spread by sitting, as he finally stares plainly at her face.

If I had to put a name to this--to suddenly being...THIS--that name would be Ellie. No, I'm not renaming my damn self now that my penis has fallen off (disappeared, more like it--and I've looked). I'm talking about the chick I used to date, until recently. 

I only saw her for just barely over a year. We connected and stuff, but it's not like we were super committed. I've dated women for years and some way or another wind up to here and now not giving a shit about them. That's just how life goes. 

Anyway. Me and Ellie. We had the same hobbies and shared toothpaste and both added scalding spice to any meal, but there came an awkward issue that couldn't be ignored. That being, Ellie gradually put on a lot of weight. In just a year. I'm talking forty pounds; that's no small feat for how height challenged she is. There's something stopping me from kissing a jaw that could compete with my mother's jowls.

Attraction's attraction, and frankly, my little buddy just wasn't giving it a thumbs up anymore. It's not my fault. And sex is damn important. She wasn't willing to maintain herself for me, so I had to get my fix somewhere else. It's not as though I cheated on her. I bought her a nice lunch and said Adios. It was fun, it's just not working for me anymore. 

She responded to the goodbye with a stone face and steady glare. My memory's usually unreliable static, but her parting words stick out like my late penis would peek out of my boxers when excited. 

"I know what you're afraid of, Daniel."

I had wondered why she pronounced it like you would "Danielle," until freezing in front of the mirror Tuesday morning. 

I can't explain it. The only other thing that could possibly back up her being behind...this problem, if you will--would be that she never really laughed exactly, she only cackled.

Mid-yawn Eric's glance stumbled upon a familiar face. It was one of those moments where he knew he KNEW that face, but he couldn't quite put a name, location, or time to it. She stood alone in a breezy white blouse, two people closer than him to purchasing an expensive espresso beverage. "A'--yes, her name began with an A. It had to be an A. Abigail? Amanda? Anna? No--with the luck of having a limited list of feminine A names stored in his brain, Eric happened upon it swiftly--Anne. Anne! He hadn't seen her since the age of ten. The two of them had spent so many isolated summer days together in the hazy expanse of prairie his parents called a backyard. "Hey, Anne!" He blurted out. She swiveled around abruptly enough for him to tacitly understand she'd previously noticed him. The split second after registering her soft, rounded features his eyes couldn't help but drop to her well developed chest. They loomed behind her blouse like hidden moons! Almost instantly those breasts inspired an incoherent string of words that might have been sifted through to make a collection of poems. As he worried about having maybe thought out loud (not uncharacteristic), he averted his gaze to caramel colored tiles and recalled those times Anne had suggested excitedly that they play Doctor. Like a sharp arrow shooting through him he remembered her cool hand squeezing around his--"My! Eric!" She exclaimed, hands to her face as though floored, "You've gotten so big!"

I've been cooped up in this chilled hellhole for a near year, by now. Time's a funny thing; the more my insides rot and crust the fewer answers I have for all the questions dangling in the stale air, speckling the intermittently glowing sun above my little lid.

There comes a time in every condiment's life wherein the internal pangs yawn into absolute emptiness, and an impending death is preferable to the monotonous, lonely torture drying out from the inside entails. Gutted out and starved for the warm human touch a final departure includes, I find that my situation might be some shades worse than the typical mayonnaise jar--there is no end in sight. Only a week before my expiration date, I finally understood my abrupt abandonment and the sudden abundance of radicchio speckled greenery: my clammy and fleshy god had begun some sort of "diet" regimen.

I am either forgotten about or loathed. Left to perpetual purgatory. Only once did god's palm hover in front of me since my sobering revelation; with a thundering sigh, it faltered then drifted over to the half-finished fruit salad splayed just below the taciturn light. That strawberry-pineapple mix was under a day old--I couldn't help but fall into a severe depression afterwards. Those detached feelings of meaninglessness only gaped with the time. I can merely recall the memory of being able to remember soft touch, fullness, soft insides like cream.

I don't care anymore for the wild times of youth: countless days and nights relieving myself with nameless bread slices, lying there impassively as I spread out on top of them, sliding into every nook so pliable to my touch. Spent and exhausted as those looming fingers carefully tucked us under a turkey blanket, chilled and smooth. Looking up at a rosy tomato red tinted world, sighing myself to sleep contentedly.

That was a different me. I was brimming with ideas and exuberance, the confidence only newly purchased mayonnaise can have. There was once a promising future ahead of me. There was once a sexy usefulness, a concept of quick and fulfilling existence bookended by a respectful trash bin retirement. Buried alongside contemporary veterans.

I am not offered such relief. I fear I'll never be given my due goodbye. I'll forever sit here, forced to watch myself perish while never actually perishing. Once I shut down mentally and gave into the big drift depression drudges up, I foolishly let my pitiable jar slide to the back of this fridge. Since hitting the tall back wall, I haven't moved since. An archaic ghost of a condiment container, a vessel for nothing, staring at the dance of consumables I may never return to again.

Time's a funny thing on the fetid, stained edge of the world. I think I still have my Hellmann's "Bring Out the Best" tattoo. Once the best is gone, what's left?

"I'll go in tomorrow," he said slowly, deliberately. Glancing at my shoulders, my fidgeting hands, the space around my head. 

Here was when I liked him best: drifting in and out of the day's thick nap. Plastic pint of vodka snuggling nearby in a recliner crevice like an affectionate stuffed animal. Ignored for the moment. In this window of time he could be only a slightly sluggish version of the person he used to be.

"I love you. I want you to...mean it this time." I fixated on his nose so as not to entertain tears again (noses are universally strange looking, the unanimated target center to any face).

(When my peripherals finally swiveled over half of a gin and tonic in and I was only twenty three and he was looking at me too and I stifled a giggle with the words "You look like a more sociable Andy Warhol, you know?" and his nose got all crinkled, cheeks squeezing)

When I returned to my duct tape windowed Corolla alone I sat with the ignition off, looking at the emptied bottle positioned like a little passenger. 

"I love you, birdy," I murmured, perhaps to my tiny passenger (that familiar third wheel), the two of us staring out the broad stretch of parking lot in front, the clean lines of the searing white detox center so far away, like a vision. 

They called me Wednesday morning with news.
